articles.title: Mother Dairy, Amul milk gets costlier: Dairy giant hikes rate by upto Rs 6 per litre from Thursday; check prices
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Milk is set to get costlier in Delhi NCR from November 12, with dairy companies Mother Dairy and Amul increasing prices by Rs 2 to Rs 6 per
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Milk is set to get costlier in Delhi NCR from November 12, with dairy companies Mother Dairy and Amul increasing prices by Rs 2 to Rs 6 per litre. The price hike comes amid lower milk supplies and higher costs of buying milk from farmers.The increase will vary across milk varieties. Toned milk will cost Rs 2 more per litre, full cream milk Rs 4 more and full cream buffalo milk Rs 6 more, according to industry sources.In Delhi-NCR, full cream packaged milk will now cost Rs 76 per litre, compared with Rs 72 earlier. Packaged toned milk will cost Rs 62, up from Rs 60, while toned milk sold through bulk vending machines will cost Rs 60 against Rs 58 earlier.Double-toned milk will become costlier from Rs 54 to Rs 56 per litre. Cow milk prices will rise from Rs 62 to Rs 65, while full cream buffalo milk, which contains 6.5% fat, will cost Rs 86 against Rs 80 earlier.Mother Dairy, the largest milk supplier in Delhi-NCR, had last increased prices on May 14, 2026.Why are milk prices increasing?Milk procurement has become more expensive for dairy companies. Milk fat prices have risen by around 20-25% over the past few months, while higher cattle feed prices have added to farmers' costs.Milk supplies have also tightened despite the flush season, when production and availability usually improve. The shortage has affected the availability of milk fat, making it more expensive for dairy companies.When fresh milk supplies fall short, companies usually use milk powder and milk fat to prepare liquid milk. However, higher milk fat prices have also increased the cost of this process.Dairy companies have raised the prices they pay farmers to encourage them to produce and supply more milk. Amul has increased the procurement rate linked to milk fat to Rs 1,000 per kilogram. This allows farmers to receive more than Rs 60 per litre for milk, according to industry sources.Mother Dairy has decided to pass on part of these higher costs to consumers. The company pays farmers 75-80% of the money it earns from milk sales, sources told PTI.How much will milk cost now?Here are the revised prices of different milk varieties in Delhi-NCR:Full cream milk (packaged): Rs 76 per litre, up from Rs 72.Toned milk (bulk vended): Rs 60 per litre, up from Rs 58.Toned milk (packaged): Rs 62 per litre, up from Rs 60.Double-toned milk: Rs 56 per litre, up from Rs 54.Cow milk: Rs 65 per litre, up from Rs 62.Full cream buffalo milk: Rs 86 per litre, up from Rs 80.Mother Dairy sells around 35 lakh litres of milk every day in Delhi-NCR through its outlets, general trade and e-commerce platforms. Its total daily milk sales across markets exceed 50 lakh litres.The company reported a 17% rise in turnover to Rs 20,300 crore in the last fiscal year. The growth was driven by higher demand for its milk products and cooking oils.Started in 1974, Mother Dairy is a wholly-owned subsidiary of the National Dairy Development Board (NDDB). It sells milk and milk products under the Mother Dairy brand, edible oils under Dhara, and fresh fruits and vegetables, frozen vegetables, snacks, pulps and concentrates under Safal.Nandini had also raised milk prices in KarnatakaBefore the latest increase by Mother Dairy and Amul, Nandini had raised milk prices in Karnataka. The state Cabinet approved an Rs 8 per litre increase in the base price, with the new rates taking effect from November 1.The Karnataka government said the increase was needed to protect dairy farmers facing severe drought conditions. Law and parliamentary affairs minister Krishna Byre Gowda said the revised prices were still within the range charged in most other states.He also said rising prices of other goods had hurt farmers and milk supply in Karnataka had fallen by 10 lakh litres due to the drought this year.Cooperation minister Laxman Savadi said the government also had to consider the possibility of farmers selling their milk to other states if prices were not increased. This could have led to a shortage of milk in Karnataka.Under the revised arrangement, Rs 7 of the Rs 8 per litre increase was to go to farmers, while Re 1 was allocated to milk unions in the state.You use AI every day. articles.title: Anthropic's $1.4 trillion IPO: Price band, listing, investors & more; all you need to know
articles.summary: The artificial intelligence (AI) boom is heading for another major test on Wall Street as Anthropic, the parent company of Claude, prepares for a mega IPO
articles.body: The artificial intelligence (AI) boom is heading for another major test on Wall Street as Anthropic, the parent company of Claude, prepares for a mega IPO targeting a valuation of $1.4 trillion.Backed by technology giants such as Amazon, Google, Nvidia and AMD, the company has seen its valuation climb rapidly. Its proposed listing will test whether public market investors share the enthusiasm that has fuelled massive investments in AI, particularly as questions grow over how quickly companies can turn their spending into profits.The shares are expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on November 19 under the ticker symbol ANT, Reuters reported.Here's what investors need to know about the proposed listing, the company's backers, its growth prospects and the risks surrounding the AI boom.Anthropic IPO: Valuation, price band, issue size and listing dateAnthropic is targeting a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, with reports suggesting its bankers are preparing to increase the figure to $1.5 trillion or more.The company plans to sell 825 million shares at $70-78 apiece, with the IPO expected to raise up to $64.4 billion. A separate private placement with cornerstone investors could bring in another $26 billion, taking the potential fundraising to $90.4 billion.At the top end of the proposed price range, Anthropic would be valued at around $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis. This includes securities such as stock options and restricted stock. Excluding these, its valuation would be close to $1 trillion.If the offering is priced at the midpoint of the proposed range, it could raise more than $61 billion.The initial terms circulated to investment banks had suggested that the IPO could raise as much as $69.3 billion. However, the updated prospectus filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission contained a lower price range and a reduced fundraising target.The shares are expected to list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on November 19 under the ticker symbol ANT.Biggest techs backing AnthropicAnthropic has attracted some of the biggest names in technology and finance, both as long-term investors and participants in its upcoming private placement.Some of its key technology backers include:InvestorInvestment and associationAmazonHas invested at least $13 billion and agreed in April to invest up to another $20 billion. Anthropic has committed to spending more than $100 billion on Amazon's cloud services over 10 years.Google (Alphabet)Has committed up to $40 billion, including an initial $10 billion investment announced in April. It also provides cloud infrastructure and AI chips used to train and run Claude models.MicrosoftHas agreed to purchase $1 billion of Anthropic's non-voting shares in the concurrent private placement.NvidiaHas agreed to purchase $10 billion of non-voting shares alongside the listing.AMDHas agreed to purchase $2.5 billion of non-voting shares.BroadcomHas agreed to purchase $1 billion of non-voting shares and is involved in financing and equipment leasing arrangements linked to Anthropic's AI infrastructure.Micron TechnologyHas agreed to purchase $1 billion of non-voting shares.TSMC PartnersHas agreed to purchase $500 million of non-voting shares.Beyond technology companies, Anthropic has received substantial backing from venture capital firms and institutional investors across multiple funding rounds. These include Spark Capital, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Fidelity Management & Research, Salesforce Ventures, ICONIQ, GIC, Coatue Management, D1 Capital Partners, Sequoia Capital, Altimeter Capital and Menlo Ventures.Among individual investors, Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn led Anthropic's first institutional funding round, a $124 million Series A in 2021. Former Google chief executive Eric Schmidt has also personally backed the company.Anthropic’s financial portfolioAnthropic's proposed listing could rank among the biggest IPOs ever, although it is expected to fall short of the $86 billion raised by SpaceX in June at a valuation of nearly $1.75 trillion.The company was last valued at $965 billion in a private funding round. Its proposed IPO valuation of up to $1.4 trillion would mark a significant jump.Its valuation is being supported by rapid growth in demand for its products, particularly its Claude models.According to its IPO filing, the company's run-rate revenue stood at roughly $81 billion as of October 31, up $10 billion from September 30.A regulatory filing last month showed that Anthropic generated more than $16 billion in revenue during the first half of the year, around 14 times its revenue in the corresponding period last year.However, the company has yet to turn a profit.Its expansion also requires enormous computing capacity. Anthropic has nearly $900 billion in computing commitments with partners, including Amazon and Google's parent Alphabet.The IPO could provide the company with significant funds to accelerate its expansion and potentially add billions of dollars to the fortunes of chief executive Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder Daniela Amodei.Anthropic was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders and is headed by Dario Amodei. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters for the offering.Anthropic and AI risks — What experts are sayingDespite strong demand for AI, investors are questioning whether heavy spending on models, data centres and computing infrastructure will generate adequate returns. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX's AI division have all lost more money than they have made, while elevated borrowing costs and regulatory concerns have added to market uncertainty. A recent Wall Street sell-off also hit stocks linked to AI infrastructure.Anthropic's IPO prospectus flags the technology's potential risks, including faster-moving competitors and safety measures failing to keep pace with AI advances. CEO Dario Amodei has called for slower development, warning in September that AI agents could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months without stronger safeguards.The proposed valuation has also drawn scrutiny from experts. "Anthropic could become an exceptionally successful company, but at this valuation, much of that success is already reflected in the price," Varun Datta, venture capitalist and founder of Truth Ventures told Reuters.Jeff Zell, senior research analyst at IPO Boutique, said the pricing could leave room for investors to bid up the shares. "By seeking a valuation close to 20% below 'market expectations', this allows investors to 'bid up' the IPO rather than facing a take-it-or-leave-it scenario like SpaceX took," he said.(Disclaimer: Recommendations and views on the stock market, other asset classes or personal finance management tips given by experts are their own. articles.title: Indian Railways steps up cleanliness checks on 11 trains with journey times of over 40 hours, staff to photograph coaches and toilets at key stops; Vivek Express, Jhelum Express on the list
articles.summary: Long-distance train journeys can sometimes be cumbersome especially on account of cleanliness in trains.
articles.body: Long-distance train journeys can sometimes be cumbersome especially on account of cleanliness in trains. The Railway Board has recently prepared a plan to tighten supervision and intensify cleanliness measures on long-distance trains that take more than 40 hours to complete their journeys.Officials have said that 11 trains have been selected under the initiative, with staff required to take photographs of coaches and toilets bearing time stamps at the starting station, destination and specified inspection points along the route.Long-distance trains in focusThe depots responsible for these trains will closely track cleanliness and maintenance, while zonal railway officials will review passenger complaints and the action taken to resolve them every week, they said.The performance of agencies providing on-board housekeeping services will also be evaluated based on complaints lodged through Rail Madad, the Railways' official digital platform."The on-board housekeeping staff in these trains will be trained to take up small repairs. Dedicated teams comprising plumbers, electrical staff and other requisite maintenance personnel may be deployed en route these trains to speedily address concerns," a senior official recently told ET. The official added that cleaning at designated 'clean train station' points would receive particular attention."Divisions have been asked to ensure adequate manpower, equipment and consumables," the official added.The 11 trains covered by the plan are Jhelum Express, Pune-Saharsa Express, Amritsar Garib Rath Express, Avadh Assam Express, Howrah-Yesvantpur Express, Vivek Express, Danapur-SMVT Bengaluru Express, Amrapali Express, Ahmedabad-Saharsa Express, Rajgir-Lokmanya Tilak Terminus Express and RKMP-Agartala Express.Indian Railways bets on waste disposalIndian Railways has put in place a comprehensive system to collect, process and dispose of waste generated at railway stations and aboard trains. Stations have been equipped with twin dustbins to facilitate waste collection and segregation at the source.Waste produced during train journeys is gathered at designated waste-handling stations at regular intervals. These stations have arrangements with Urban Local Bodies and municipal authorities to ensure its proper disposal.Depending on operational requirements, Indian Railways has also installed waste-processing facilities at various stations, including biogas and composting plants, as well as plastic bottle-crushing machines.Following the applicability of the new Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, and directions issued by the Supreme Court, the Railways has undertaken several initiatives to strengthen waste management across its establishments.The Railway Board has issued a Standard Operating Procedure (SoP) for solid waste management across railway stations, trains, railway colonies, hospitals, workshops, production units and other railway establishments. The guidelines lay down procedures for waste segregation, collection, transportation, processing and scientific disposal. They also specify monitoring arrangements and clearly define responsibilities at different levels of the administration.Zonal Railways have begun identifying units that fall under the category of bulk waste generators as defined by the SWM Rules, 2026. An “As-is Waste Characterization and Quantification Study” has also been planned to evaluate the existing volume and composition of waste generated across Indian Railways' establishments and trains.Dedicated nodal officers have been appointed by Zonal Railways to draw up comprehensive waste management plans, carry out periodic audits, oversee implementation and submit regular compliance reports to the Railway Board. Divisions have also been instructed to formulate their own action plans to improve waste management. In addition, dedicated Environment & Housekeeping Management (EnHM) departments have been set up at the divisional, zonal and Railway Board levels to oversee waste management-related issues.To maintain cleanliness and hygiene throughout train journeys, Indian Railways provides on-board housekeeping services (OBHS) on 1,450 pairs of identified long-distance trains.The Clean Train Station (CTS) scheme is operational at 63 stations and covers 2,800 trains. Under this arrangement, dedicated teams equipped with cleaning equipment use the scheduled halts to clean coach toilets and washbasins and remove garbage from dustbins inside the trains.You use AI every day. articles.title: Blackstone to buy 16% in IIFL Finance for Rs 5,000 crore: What's the deal all about
articles.summary: Global investment firm Blackstone is set to buy nearly 16% stake in IIFL Finance for Rs 5,000 crore.
articles.body: Global investment firm Blackstone is set to buy nearly 16% stake in IIFL Finance for Rs 5,000 crore. The investment is part of a larger Rs 6,414 crore fundraise approved by the company's board on Tuesday.The deal will make Blackstone a key investor in the non-bank lender, which plans to use the fresh capital to strengthen its finances and expand its lending business, particularly gold loans and credit to small businesses.The Rs 6,414 crore fundraise will come from three investors. Blackstone will contribute Rs 5,000 crore, while IIFL Finance's promoters, Nirmal Jain and R Venkataraman, will invest Rs 1,264 crore. Anchorage Capital will put in another Rs 150 crore.Breaking down the Blackstone dealAccording to the company's stock exchange filing, funds managed by Blackstone Private Equity will invest through a preferential allotment of compulsorily convertible preference shares. These shares will be converted into equity shares at Rs 602 apiece within 18 months of allotment.After the conversion, Blackstone will hold approximately 16% of IIFL Finance on a fully diluted basis.Blackstone will also get representation on the company's board. However, the existing promoters will continue as co-promoters, and IIFL Finance has clarified that the deal will not lead to a change in control.Where will the fresh capital go? The fresh capital is expected to improve the company's financial position and give it more room to grow its lending business.IIFL Finance expects its capital adequacy ratio to rise to around 30% from nearly 17%, based on September 2026 figures. The additional funds will mainly support its secured lending businesses, particularly gold finance, along with lending to small businesses.The company also plans to invest more in technology and expand its co-lending partnerships with banks. It said the stronger capital base could help improve its credit ratings and lower borrowing costs over time.Welcoming Blackstone as an investor, IIFL Finance Founder and Managing Director Nirmal Jain said, "We are delighted to welcome Blackstone as a partner in IIFL Finance. Their investment is a strong endorsement of the franchise our team has built, and of the opportunity to bring formal, secured credit to millions of underserved households and small businesses across India."Jain added, "The investment strengthens our balance sheet and gives us the headroom to scale our franchises, invest further in technology, and deepen our co-lending partnerships with banks, while staying disciplined on risk and capital."IIFL Finance's portfolioIIFL Finance had assets under management of Rs 1.24 lakh crore on a consolidated basis as of September-end. Its gross non-performing assets stood at 1.5% of total loans, down 7 basis points from three months earlier.Blackstone's investment comes amid a series of deals involving global financial firms and Indian lenders.Canada's Fairfax Financial Holdings has proposed buying a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank. Bank of America has bought a 49.9% stake in the non-bank lending arm of Jio Financial Services, while Japan's MUFG has invested in Shriram Finance. Dubai-based Emirates NBD has also agreed to buy a 60% stake in RBL Bank.The proposed investment in IIFL Finance is subject to regulatory and shareholder approvals.You use AI every day. articles.title: Exclusive-Military-linked Chinese university bought Nvidia H200 chips despite US blacklist, records show
articles.summary: BEIJING, Nov 11 (Reuters) - A Chinese university with deep ties to the People's Liberation Army bought Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips last month despite bei...
articles.body:
BEIJING, Nov 11 (Reuters) - A Chinese university with deep ties to the People's Liberation Army bought Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show, highlighting gaps in Washington's efforts to curb China's access to advanced technology.

The findings come as Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang face mounting scrutiny in Washington over his lobbying for looser restrictions on sales ‌of AI chips to China, following reports alleging he was targeted by a Chinese spying operation.

Huang has argued that continued US sales to China would preserve American technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on US technology. ‌But some US lawmakers say access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips can speed China's development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation.

Both Democrats and Republicans in Congress have urged stronger controls on China's access to advanced AI chips, such as chip-tracking requirements and greater congressional oversight ​of exports. Three Republican congressional committee chairmen have requested a briefing with Huang on November 18 over his reported contacts with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative.

Northwestern Polytechnical University bought two H200 chips last month for 874,700 yuan ($123,000), according to an October 21 procurement record on its website.

Northwestern is a member of the "Seven Sons of National Defense" group of Chinese universities under U.S. sanctions and with a history of conducting defence-related research for Beijing.

The chips were purchased for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record shows.

The H200 is among Nvidia's most capable chips for training and running advanced AI systems and is subject to US export licence approvals, which are normally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical.

Northwestern Polytechnical also bought access this year to ‌H200 chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five contracts for rented computing capacity ⁠from Chinese companies, procurement records show.

Reuters is reporting the chip purchases and computing contracts for the first time. Northwestern Polytechnical, Nvidia and the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees export controls, did not respond to requests for comment. Reuters could not determine contact details for Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology.

articles.title: Insurer rejected Rs 30 lakh accidental death claim citing alcohol consumption; consumer commission finds medical record discrepancies and upholds payout with 9% interest and Rs 75,000 as compensation
articles.summary: Insurance payouts can sometimes be tricky if the insurer denies claims.
articles.body: Insurance payouts can sometimes be tricky if the insurer denies claims. In one such case, a pensioner died following a road accident and his wife and two daughters turned to the accidental death insurance cover associated with his pension account for financial assistance.However, the insurer declined their claim, citing a policy clause excluding certain injuries linked to alcohol consumption. The family challenged the insurer's decision and won relief.What the case is aboutA pensioner held coverage under a group personal accident/salary package/pension account policy issued by the insurer through the man’s bank account.The insurance policy covered the period from January 4, 2022, to January 3, 2023. On April 9, 2022, the man was involved in a motor accident and suffered severe head injuries. He was taken to a hospital, where he died on April 18, 2022.His wife and two daughters filed a claim for the insured amount of Rs 30 lakh on December 5, 2022. The insurer however, rejected their request on January 9, 2023, relying on a policy exclusion concerning injuries sustained under the influence of alcohol.“The insurer relied on the policy exclusion for being under the influence of intoxicating liquor or drugs or other intoxicants except where the insured is not directly responsible for the injury/accident though under influence of intoxication,” says Vishal Jain, Founder and Senior Partner at Ayaam Legal.The family contested the insurer's decision before the District Consumer Commission, Vellore. They argued that it had repudiated the claim without presenting credible medical or scientific evidence to establish that the man was intoxicated at the time of the accident.The District Commission ruled in the family's favour, directing the insurer to settle the insurance claim and pay interest and compensation for deficiency in service and mental agony. The insurer then appealed against the order before the Tamil Nadu State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission.Why did the family win the case against the insurer?The State Commission upheld the District Commission's order directing the insurer to settle the accidental death insurance claim of Rs 30 lakh.The insurer was also ordered to pay annual interest at 9% from September 1, 2023, until the date of the District Commission's order. In addition, the family was awarded Rs 50,000 as compensation for deficiency in service and mental agony, along with Rs 25,000 towards litigation expenses.The Commission found several significant gaps in the evidence presented by the insurer.According to Vivek Kumar, Advocate, Delhi High Court, the insurer based its decision partly on a hospital death summary that stated that the deceased was under the influence of alcohol when the incident occurred.However, the Commission noted that the medical document did not clarify the basis for this statement. It was unclear whether the information came from the deceased himself, an accompanying person, the police or another medico-legal source, or an independent clinical assessment by the treating doctor.The Commission stressed that recording a patient's history of alcohol consumption does not, by itself, establish that the person was under the influence of alcohol at the relevant time.The insurer also cited a reported plasma alcohol level of 106.1 mg/dL. However, the insurer did not submit the original laboratory report to establish the identity and nature of the blood specimen, when it had been collected, which laboratory had tested it, the relevant report or sample number, or whether the test result could be linked to the deceased.The Commission observed that a numerical reading, even when stated with precision, cannot automatically be accepted as scientifically established evidence unless its source and authenticity are demonstrated.Another important aspect of the ruling was the Commission's examination of the two death summaries placed before it by the parties. One of the most significant inconsistencies concerned the date of death. The document relied upon by the insurer recorded April 11, 2022, as the date of death. However, the admitted facts and the medical record submitted by the complainants established that the man had died on April 18, 2022, Kumar told ET.According to the Commission, such discrepancies had a material bearing on the reliability of the documents, the identification of the records and their chronological traceability.The Commission also reiterated that an insurer seeking to reject a claim by invoking an exclusion clause must establish the factual circumstances required for that exclusion to apply. The burden was not on the family to explain or disprove every inconsistency left unresolved in the insurer's documents.The Commission further referred to the Supreme Court's judgment in IFFCO Tokio General Insurance Company Ltd. v. Pearl Beverages Ltd., AIR 2021 SC 2277. The ruling clarifies that an insurer is not required in every case to produce a breathalyser reading or a blood-alcohol test report to establish that an exclusion applies. The conclusion can instead be based on the totality of reliable circumstances, Kumar explains.However, this does not absolve an insurer of the responsibility to establish that the insured was actually under the influence of alcohol.You use AI every day. articles.title: Trump’s peaceful mood doesn’t fully explain why energy prices are plunging
articles.summary: The simple political explanation for such a dramatic decline in oil prices fails to account for the astonishing changes happening under the oil market’s hood.
articles.body: This was supposed to be the week that America dramatically escalated its war with Iran. President Donald Trump repeatedly hinted that US and Israeli attacks on Iran would resume once the midterm elections were over. In anticipation of a military escalation, oil prices spent every single day of October above $100 a barrel, gradually rising to a four-year high of $114 on the last trading day of the month. Then, a sudden shift: Trump just before the midterms argued that renewed attacks were no longer necessary. And, last Tuesday, Americans voted overwhelmingly for Democrats in a sweeping rebuke of Trump’s Iran policy – a signal that Congress may put up some resistance to the war. Oil prices plunged over the past week, sinking by $25 to their lowest point in three months and briefly falling below $90 a barrel Tuesday. Are those events related? Undoubtedly. But the simple political explanation for such a dramatic decline in oil prices fails to account for the astonishing changes happening under the oil market’s hood: Despite the biggest oil supply shock in history, the world is suddenly producing more crude than it consumes. The oil market has returned to its fundamentals, and they’re looking surprisingly strong. The market always finds a way The story of the oil market throughout the Iran war has been one of remarkable creativity. Many oil analysts anticipated doomsday scenarios of oil quickly topping $200 a barrel when Iran blocked off tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz pinch point. Instead, oil never came close to hitting the all-time high set in 2008 – or even the more recent peak set in 2022 at the outset of the Russia-Ukraine war. The market’s resourcefulness – rerouting oil via pipelines and forcing crude tankers through the strait via complex shuttle and military operations – paid off. During occasional days over the past couple months, oil flows through the Middle East have surpassed pre-war averages. Middle Eastern oil transits certainly haven’t returned to normal. The flows have been volatile, and they were averaging 70% of the pre-war average over the past week, according to oil data tracker Kpler. But after plunging to 9.8 million barrels per day at the outset of the war in March, oil transits averaged 20.7 million barrels per day last week, according to Natasha Kaneva, head of global commodities research at JPMorgan. That’s closing in on the 24.7 million barrels the Middle East was shipping each day before the war. (Math time: 20.7 million – 24.7 million = -4 million. Keep that in the back of your head.) To compensate, oil majors increased output from around the world – particularly from Latin America. Crude flows from outside the Middle East grew by 1.5 million barrels per day from the same point last year. (More math: -4 million+ 1.5 million = -2.5 million. Keep reading.) Those increases have been gradual but steady (unlike the topsy turvy Middle East), and energy companies continue to see promise there: Exxon announced Tuesday it has taken preliminary steps that could eventually lead it to return to Venezuela after a two-decade hiatus. But we’re still at -2.5 million barrels per day. The increase in global production and brute force through the Middle East don’t fully account for how the oil market could return to balance. From shock to surplus The missing element: plunging demand. Oil consumption has fallen by 3.3 million barrels per day on average during the course of the war, according to JPMorgan, and demand has grown considerably worse over the past couple months. Consumption fell by 3.8 million barrels per day in September and October. (Last math: -2.5 million + 3.8 million = 1.3 million barrels per day. … OK with rounding it’s actually 1.4 million, but whatever.) So that’s how you get to an October oil surplus: Stop using as much oil. The decline in oil demand was in part because high prices forced consumers around the world to make some painful decisions about their energy usage. But fuel prices factored in less to the oil surplus than you might think. Yes, diesel hit a record high several weeks ago as Ukraine bombarded Russian refineries with drone strikes – until a Trump-negotiated energy ceasefire led to a multi-week respite. And gas prices are on track for a four-year high in 2026, even as they fell below $4 on Tuesday for the first time in several months. It’s also true that gasoline demand has been in a yearslong slump; electric vehicles are growing increasingly popular – outside the United States, that is; and fuel economy is improving. Improved mileage has put annual per-capita American gas consumption on pace to fall to a post-pandemic low of 390 gallons this year, down from 440 gallons a decade ago, according to Pavel Molchanov, investment strategy analyst at Raymond James. But both diesel and gas demand slumped primarily for a less obvious reason: refinery constraints. The world simply doesn’t have sufficient refinery infrastructure to make up for lost output from the Middle East and Russia. Global refineries have been working in overdrive. The world could produce all the oil it wants, but it simply can’t make it into useful fuels fast enough. So, the refining shortfall has been absorbed by sinking global demand – for gas, diesel and the oil that would otherwise be refined into fuel. Who has leverage now? The oil surplus has allowed the US to replenish some of its key inventories – particularly in Cushing, Oklahoma, the pipeline crossroads of America. Cushing stockpiles fell below operational minimums in July and are now at their highest level since May, according to the US Energy Information Administration. That gives the key storage facility some much-needed wiggle room, staving off a potential oil price crisis. A month or two of oil surplus building could give Trump some leverage to wait Iran out. The US-led blockade against Iran’s ports is working: Iran has exported zero oil through legitimate channels since August, and the economic embargo has sent Iran’s annual inflation rate surging above 70% over the past year – the country’s highest since World War II. And a Democratic Congress may be able to hold Trump back a bit, but lawmakers will lack significant power to get out of the Iran war. Still, the “blue tsunami” showed that Iran maintains leverage, too: Trump has been politically weakened, and the election showed Iran can inflict significant economic damage across the world by maintaining a military presence in the Strait of Hormuz. “This is not a recipe for a quick, acceptable end to the conflict,” said Dan Pickering, founder and chief investment officer at Pickering Energy Partners. “This is a recipe for more of the same.”

articles.title: Russia's oil game runs dry as Ukrainian drones knock out 30% of refining capacity
articles.summary: A series of Ukrainian drone attacks has knocked out a significant chunk of Russia's oil refining capacity, with operations affected at nine of the
articles.body: A series of Ukrainian drone attacks has knocked out a significant chunk of Russia's oil refining capacity, with operations affected at nine of the country's 35 major refineries over the past week. The strikes have reduced Russia's refining capacity by around 30% since late October, according to two industry sources. The attacks have affected facilities with a combined daily nameplate capacity of around 300,000 metric tonnes, or 2.2 million barrels.These include three major refineries in central Russia, as well as plants in Ryazan, Yaroslavl and the Volga region. Russia has a total primary refining capacity of approximately 930,000 tonnes per day.However, its refineries were processing around 700,000 tonnes, or five million barrels, of crude oil daily at the end of October. Industry sources estimate that the actual reduction in daily crude processing could reach 200,000 tonnes.The attacks have also added to Moscow's difficulties in tackling domestic fuel shortages while continuing to ship diesel to international markets under an export deal with US President Donald Trump.Ukraine intensified its strikes on Russian oil facilities after a proposed ceasefire on attacks against energy infrastructure, announced by Trump between Kyiv and Moscow in late October, failed to take effect.In the latest attack, on Wednesday, a Ukrainian drone hit the Kirishi oil refinery, Russia's second-largest, on Monday night. The strike triggered a fire at the facility and killed a woman, the governor of the Leningrad region said.Meanwhile, Russian forces continued targeting Ukraine's energy and transport infrastructure. Prime minister Sergii Koretskyi said on Wednesday that six large electricity substations across four central Ukrainian regions had been struck.In a post on Telegram, he also reported attacks on railway infrastructure in eastern and central Ukraine.The exchange of attacks has also drawn criticism from both sides over the proposed halt to strikes on energy facilities.Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov, in an article published in the daily newspaper Kommersant on Tuesday, said Ukraine was ignoring Trump's calls to stop attacks on Russian energy targets.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, however, said last week that Kyiv would continue striking targets linked to Russia's oil sector in retaliation for Moscow's attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.He said Ukrainian power plants, energy networks, heating systems and water supply systems were under constant attack, adding that Moscow had "refused the de-escalation steps that our partners talked about".You use AI every day. articles.title: Noida Metro extension to Rs 3,230 crore national museum project: Cabinet approves key 5 decisions
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved five major decisions, including the extension of the Aqua Line Metro corridor from Noida Sector 51 to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved five major decisions, including the extension of the Aqua Line Metro corridor from Noida Sector 51 to Greater Noida Sector 4, the development of the Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum in the North and South Block buildings in Delhi, and a Rs 62,370 crore fertiliser subsidy for the 2026-27 rabi season.The Cabinet also approved the continuation of credit guarantee schemes to support micro entrepreneurs, as well as women and entrepreneurs from Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.Briefing reporters after the Cabinet meeting, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said the decisions were aimed at strengthening infrastructure, supporting farmers and encouraging entrepreneurship."Today, PM Narendra Modi took five major decisions in the Cabinet. The first is the establishment of a new Yuge Yugeen Bharat National Museum, which will showcase India's cultural heritage in a very beautiful manner. It will be the world's largest museum. Second, the Cabinet has approved a metro rail project from Noida to Greater Noida. Third, a fertiliser subsidy of Rs 62,370 crore has been approved for our farmers for the Rabi season. Fourth, a credit guarantee fund of Rs 5,000 crore has been approved under the MUDRA scheme for young people aspiring to become entrepreneurs. A credit guarantee fund of Rs 4,111 crore has also been approved under the Stand-Up India scheme for SC, ST and women entrepreneurs..." he said.Aqua Line to be extended to Greater Noida Sector 4The Cabinet approved the extension of the Noida-Greater Noida Metro's Aqua Line from Noida Sector 51 to Greater Noida Sector 4 at an estimated cost of Rs 2,390 crore.The 8.449-km corridor will have five elevated stations and is expected to be completed in four years. Once operational, it will take the combined active metro network in Noida and Greater Noida to 71.878 km, according to an official statement.Vaishnaw said the extension would improve connectivity to IT companies and global capability centres in the area, while also linking commuters to other parts of Delhi and the airport."The second decision taken today is regarding metro connectivity between Noida and Greater Noida. If we look at this map, you can see the Aqua Line. The new project approved today will extend the line from Noida Sector 51 to Greater Noida Sector 4. Several IT industries and Global Capability Centres (GCCs) are established in this area, and this project will provide connectivity to all of them. Once the Aqua Line is extended, it will also provide connectivity to other parts of Delhi and the airport," he said.Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum to be world's largestThe Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) approved Rs 3,230 crore for the development of the Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum in the historic North and South Block complex in New Delhi.The project will involve the adaptive reuse of the two buildings, preserving their architectural character and heritage significance while converting them into a public cultural institution.Spread across a proposed built-up area of around 1,78,509 square metres, the museum will showcase India's civilisational heritage through displays of its tangible and intangible cultural traditions. It will use contemporary museum practices, immersive technologies and visitor-focused interpretation.The government has described it as a potential global landmark, with the world's largest museum display area.Rs 62,370 crore fertiliser subsidy for rabi seasonThe Cabinet approved a subsidy of Rs 62,370 crore on phosphatic and potassic (P&K) fertilisers for the 2026-27 rabi season, covering the period from October 2026 to March 31, 2027.The subsidy will be provided under the Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) scheme for fertilisers, including di-ammonium phosphate (DAP) and NPKS grades, to ensure their availability to farmers at affordable prices.Vaishnaw said fertiliser prices had risen sharply due to the West Asia crisis and the Russia-Ukraine war. The government, he said, would absorb the additional burden to protect farmers. He also said the retail price of a 50-kg bag of DAP would remain unchanged at Rs 1,350.Credit guarantee schemes extendedThe Cabinet approved the extension of the Credit Guarantee Fund for Micro Units (CGFMU) until March 2031, continuing collateral-free credit support under the Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana (PMMY).The scheme provides credit guarantee coverage to lending institutions through the National Credit Guarantee Trustee Company Limited (NCGTC), protecting them against the risk of loan defaults.Since the launch of PMMY, more than 60.36 crore loans worth Rs 43.34 lakh crore had been sanctioned by lending institutions as of September 2026. The Cabinet also approved a Rs 5,000-crore corpus to facilitate PMMY loans amounting to Rs 12.6 lakh crore, an official release said. Launched in January 2016, CGFMU has played a key role in supporting the growth of Mudra loans, the release added.Rs 4,111 crore fund for SC, ST and women entrepreneursThe Cabinet also approved the continuation of the credit guarantee fund under the Stand-Up India scheme for five years. The Rs 4,111-crore fund will support women and entrepreneurs from Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: What 400 years of hot IPOs say about buying Anthropic on day one: Chart of the Day
articles.summary: From the Dutch East India Company to Cerebras, IPO buyers have usually been rewarded for patience, not speed.
articles.body:
Anthropic's roadshow is selling the future of AI. Four centuries of hot IPOs say the first trade is rarely the best one.

The AI lab is asking for as much as $1.4 trillion at the top of its $70-to-$78 range, counting every possible share . Trading could start as soon as next week. Rival OpenAI ( OPAI.PRV ) may not be far behind: OpenAI president Greg Brockman said last week the company could be ready to go public next year.

History has a warning for anyone planning to buy on the first day . The world's first IPO, the Dutch East India Company, began trading in 1602. Its stock took about three decades to double .

This year brought two fresh reminders. SpaceX ( SPCX ) opened at $150 in June, $15 above its IPO price, and soared about 40% in its first week. By August, it was in a nearly 30% hole. Five months later, SpaceX is still below its first trade.

Cerebras ( CBRS ) had it worse. The AI chipmaker opened at nearly double its $185 IPO price in May. Its first close is still its best, and the stock now trades at about half what IPO buyers paid.

Anthropic's growth is anything but typical. Revenue in the first nine months of the year was 13 times what it was a year earlier. But investors are being asked to pay up for it. At $78 a share, Anthropic would trade at about 29 times its sales over the past year, by Yahoo Finance calculations.

University of Florida professor Jay Ritter tracked more than 4,000 IPOs of companies with at least $100 million in sales since 1980. Those priced at 20 to 40 times sales gained about 3% on average over three years from their first close. The cheapest gained about 41%.

There's a bright spot for Anthropic. IPOs of the biggest companies, those with more than $1 billion in sales, did about as well as the market.

A big first-day pop would make the math worse. A jump of about 40% would push Anthropic past 40 times sales, where IPOs lost nearly half their value over three years.

That pop goes to whoever buys at the IPO offering price , usually big Wall Street firms and their wealthy clients. It has averaged nearly 20% since 1975, Ritter's data shows, and everyone buying after the open pays for it. This time, Anthropic is setting aside up to a fifth of its shares for retail brokers including Schwab, Fidelity, and Robinhood.

Other companies are racing to sell stock before the deal, competing for the same investors' dollars. "The Anthropic IPO is almost becoming this magnet where everybody's trying to raise liquidity in front of them," Peachtree Creek Investments founder Conor Sen said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang in November.

articles.title: Inside Democrats’ plan to put Wall Street on trial over Jeffrey Epstein
articles.summary: Democrats on Capitol Hill are vowing to probe major banks with ties to deceased convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein once their new congressional majorities become official in January. Those investigations, Democrats say, will provide insight into whether executives at financial institutions, such as JPMorgan Chase, Deutsche Bank and Bank of America, were aware of or…
articles.body:
Democrats on Capitol Hill are vowing to probe major banks with ties to deceased convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein once their new congressional majorities become official in January.

Those investigations, Democrats say, will provide insight into whether executives at financial institutions, such as JPMorgan Chase, Deutsche Bank and Bank of America, were aware of or even facilitated Epstein’s crimes .

“I feel very strongly about this, because we’ve got three Wall Street banks who, if they had done nothing … except follow the law for years on end, we could have stopped Epstein cold,” Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) told reporters Monday.

Wyden, who is in line to chair the Senate Finance Committee come January, added he will “use all the tools” at his disposal to probe the banks, including by subpoenaing top executives.

“I don’t know for sure who should be held accountable, who was responsible for what, but we’re going to look into all of it,” Rep. Mike Quigley (D-Ill.) told The Hill on Tuesday.

Federal investigators, lawmakers and victims of Epstein have long scrutinized the role major banks played in the crimes of the disgraced financier, who died in 2019.

Democrats also criticized the Trump administration’s handling of the files related to Epstein dating back to last summer, with the party’s sweeping midterm victories ushering in a new era of oversight on Capitol Hill.

“There has to be a complete investigation of that entire [situation],” Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) told The Hill on Tuesday.

In August, Wyden released a report accusing Bank of America, Deutsche Bank and JPMorgan Chase of violating federal anti-money laundering laws by “failing to screen and report Epstein’s suspicious financial transactions in a timely manner.”

Bank of America “likely violated” federal anti-money laundering laws by “failing to properly screen and report” $170 million in payments that Epstein received from investor Leon Black, the report alleged.

Deutsche Bank, meanwhile, allegedly ignored “massive withdrawals of cash for questionable purposes” from Epstein’s accounts.

JPMorgan Chase also “likely” violated federal law by “underreporting” Epstein’s suspicious financial activity to the Treasury Department, while its executives “had knowledge of” the presence of young women or underage girls at Epstein’s homes, per the report.

The GOP-led House Oversight Committee’s report on the government’s handling of the Epstein case, which the panel released Tuesday, said JPMorgan Chase flagged most of the suspicious transactions involving the financier only after federal authorities arrested him in 2019.

“Upholding a network of prominence to cover a vast array of criminal sexual activity took more than a few individuals to achieve,” the report stated, noting JPMorgan Chase and Deutsche Bank kept Epstein as a client after his 2008 conviction on soliciting a minor for prostitution.

A spokesperson for JPMorgan Chase, along with a spokesperson for Bank of America, did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment. A spokesperson for Deutsche Bank declined to comment.

In recent years, the three banks have agreed to pay Epstein’s victims a combined $437.5 million via settled lawsuits.

Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia (Calif.), the incoming chair of the House Oversight panel, has vowed to conduct his own investigation into the Epstein case once he takes the gavel.

“It is shameful that those currently in charge have not held one hearing on the Jeffrey Epstein investigation in the U.S. House, not one public hearing,” Garcia told reporters last week, the day after Democrats clinched control of the Senate and House .

The California Democrat, along with Democrats from both chambers and GOP Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.), also introduced legislation last month that proposes requiring federal financial regulators to publicly disclose supervisory records related to Epstein and his associates.

The bill, titled the “Epstein Wall Street Records Act,” would additionally require regulators, including the Federal Reserve and the Securities and Exchange Commission, to investigate banks and executives linked to the deceased sex offender.

Democrats, including members of the incoming freshman class , argue that probing banks linked to Epstein is a tenet of their quest to restore Americans’ trust in government.

“There’s a lot of interest in making the connection between the forms of corruption that people can make with their eyes … whether that’s the trafficking in the Epstein files or … all the Trumpian corruption,” Rep.-elect Brad Lander (D-N.Y.) told The Hill on Monday.

Lander, who said the House Financial Services Committee should look into banks’ links to Epstein, said those who “knowingly financed trafficking” should face congressional inquiries.

“There’s just a lot of people who are still wondering, ‘What the hell went down? What’s going on with the millions of files that still haven’t been released?’ So, I think we need an entire review of that,” Rep.-elect Dan Koh (D-Mass.) said Monday.

As for whether that should feature bank executives testifying to Congress, Koh replied, “Whatever it takes.”

Other Democrats highlighted the need to expose those who were aware of or took part in Epstein’s crimes.

To do so, lawmakers must take an “all of the above strategy” to their Epstein investigation, Rep. Veronica Escobar (D-Texas) told The Hill.

“It was a very sophisticated, complex web of co-conspirators,” she said. “And we really do need to root that out.”

The Texas Democrat added she would “applaud” the House Oversight panel subpoenaing bank executives.

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez (D-N.M.), the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said a probe into banks should “absolutely” be a focus for lawmakers, adding Epstein survivors have said to “follow” the money.

“We want to be able to follow the money, because that’s the part of corruption and that’s the part of power that Americans are so angry about,” the New Mexico Democrat told The Hill. “That the rich and powerful get away with crime.”

“What you do is you follow the money,” she reiterated “… Who was involved? So, exactly who that is, you follow it wherever it leads.”

articles.title: AI data center opponents are cheering midterm results, but they say the fight isn’t over
articles.summary: Texas resident Maggie Elizabeth Hill stayed up late on election night to watch the midterm results trickle in. But she was up early again the next morning, already thinking about how she could work with the state’s newly elected Democratic leaders to slow the development of AI data centers.
articles.body: Texas resident Maggie Elizabeth Hill stayed up late on election night to watch the midterm results trickle in. But she was up early again the next morning, already thinking about how she could work with the state’s newly elected Democratic leaders to slow the development of AI data centers. “I was so excited with the results,” said Hill, who earlier this year formed the data center watchdog group Don’t Drain Texas to help rural communities push back on data center projects. “I started brainstorming like, what can the lieutenant governor do? What are our routes to success here?” The rapid buildout of AI data centers became a central issue in the months leading up to the midterms. Grassroots campaigns cropped up in communities nationwide, raising concerns about the local implications of massive new AI data center projects. Much of the resistance also served as an outlet for general distrust of AI and frustration with the power and wealth of tech billionaires. Like Hill, data center opponents across the country see last week’s election results — where a staggering wave of populist, Democratic candidates won even in typically red stronghold areas — as a referendum on the issue and a significant win for their movement. They say concerns about AI data centers hiking electricity costs, harming the environment and impacting the livability of nearby communities drove members of their communities to the polls. Nationwide, about a quarter of American voters said AI and data centers were “crucial” to their vote in the midterms, CNN’s Voter Poll found. When asked about building data centers in their communities, voters were opposed by a roughly 3-to-1 margin. But data center opponents say the fight isn’t over. Now, they will work to hold these newly elected officials accountable for their promises to rein in or put new guardrails around data center construction — or push them to take even harder lines. Many are seeking moratoriums on data center construction, but some simply want more transparency and greater benefits for nearby residents baked into the development process. “I am an independent, and I definitely voted with… data centers at the top of my list, and I know so many people who are from rural communities who traditionally vote Republican who said that this was flipping them,” Hill told CNN. A key election issue Multiple candidates succeeded in tough races after making data centers central to their campaigns, including Democratic Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Annie Andrews of South Carolina. Democrats pulled off a massive upset in Hill’s state of Texas, winning the state’s high-profile Senate race and unseating Republican incumbents for governor and lieutenant governor. “When the politicians stop speaking for the people or being responsive to the people, you’re going to see a recalibration, and I believe that happened certainly” in the midterms, said Nick Owens, an attorney who founded Conserve Ohio, a group that opposes large data center construction. Owens, a lifelong Republican and delegate for President Donald Trump at the 2024 Republican National Convention, added that Democrats “1,000%” did a better job speaking to voters about data centers ahead of the election. Meanwhile, GOP candidates had to contend with a link to Trump, who has dismissed concerns around data centers as a “hoax” and said communities who oppose them must want to be “backwards and poor.” In Ohio, Democratic Gov.-elect Amy Acton ran on a “conditional moratorium” on data center development, which would require developers to cover energy generation costs and commit to transparency measures, among other guardrails, to have their projects approved. But Owens said his group would push her to go further — using New York Gov. Kathy Hochul’s one-year moratorium on new AI data center construction in her state as a model. He’s also hopeful that Brown could contribute to progress on federal legislation around data centers, given his previous experience in the Senate. ‘Our fight doesn’t change’ Across the country, many activists oppose data centers because they want to preserve their community’s land and natural resources. That’s what motivates Nancy Thellman, whose family farm in an agricultural part of Douglas County, Kansas, is around a 15-minute drive away from a proposed hyperscale data center project. “We have people who are trying so hard to keep their farms, to keep their skills, to keep the next generation on the farm, so that food can be grown,” Thellman said. She’s concerned about “data centers coming in and taking vast swaths of prime farmland out of production for a purpose that is not entirely understood or known for the future.” Thellman and her grassroots group, the Douglas County Data Center Watchdogs, are optimistic that the election results in Kansas will give them a greater shot at pushing state legislators to revise or rescind controversial state Senate Bill 98, which passed last year, giving tax exemptions to data center developers. Kansas last week elected its first Democratic senator in more than 90 years, as well as a Democratic attorney general. Democrat Cindy Holscher is in the lead for governor as the final votes are counted. Holscher, formerly a state senator, was among those who approved Senate Bill 98. But Thellman said she discussed the issue with Holscher during a cold campaign call from the gubernatorial candidate and was convinced the politician had changed her view. Holscher’s campaign site calls for a pause on data center development until more guardrails can be put in place and states that “big corporations don’t deserve taxpayer handouts.” “She saw the error in that vote, and she made it very clear that should she be governor, she would place a statewide moratorium on data center development until reasonable guardrails could be put up,” Thellman said. “She was a politician who is brave enough and wise enough to change her mind and promise to legislate in a different way… We’ll hold her to it.” Danielle Ray, lead organizer with the Louisville, Kentucky-based advocacy group No Data Center 502, told CNN that “our fight doesn’t change” following the election, although Democrats flipped nine seats in the statehouse. The group is fighting to stop a more than 1 million-square-foot data center project in the city. “I believe that this has been part of the reason that some of the seats have been flipped in Kentucky,” Ray said. “But I think our concern is that it might cause folks to relax or think that the fight is over just because you know Democrats won (the) majority across the country.”

articles.title: A new fire-suppression system fights flames with sound waves
articles.summary: Sonic Fire Tech has developed a technology it says can extinguish fires without causing water damage to homes.
articles.body: Forget water: An Ohio company has found a way to fight fires with sound waves. The technology could extinguish a blaze without drenching your home or business. Each year, there are around 330,000 home fires in the US, resulting in 2,600 civilian deaths. While the number of home fires has halved since 1980, fire fighters today are facing new challenges. Modern homes experience more grease-related fires, with more people cooking with oil than in the past. Lithium-ion batteries are becoming increasingly common — which the US Department of Commerce says have caused more than 200,000 fires since 2011 Now, Sonic Fire Tech has developed a technology it says can extinguish fires without drawing on strained municipal water supplies or causing water damage — using low-frequency sound waves. Acoustic suppression The company has developed an acoustic generator that can be housed inside a building, and produces high-pressure infrasound waves. These travel through a dedicated ducting system, much like plumbing or HVAC. Sonic Fire Tech says the sound waves vibrate oxygen molecules and push them away faster than the fuel can use them. Since fire needs oxygen to sustain itself, without it, the flames starve. “We want to fight fires without the inconveniences of conventional suppression,” co-founder and CEO of Sonic Fire Tech Geoff Bruder said. “A traditional sprinkler triggers when it senses heat between 135 and 165 degrees Fahrenheit, which takes at least three minutes of burning fire. And then, it unleashes 8 to 24 gallons of water per minute into the room it’s installed in.” Sonic Fire Tech’s system activates the moment it detects heat. Because sound waves cause no damage to the building, there’s no reason to wait; if it’s a false alarm, there’s no harm done. The sound waves are below the audible range of 20 Hz, so humans and pets can’t hear them. “What makes our system especially promising is that it can suppress grease fires — something water-based systems can’t do,” Bruder said. The estimated installation cost for a 3,500 square feet home is $30,000 or around $8.50 per square foot. The US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) has previously studied the idea of using sound to suppress fires, and a decade ago students at George Mason University found a way to miniaturize the technology. But Bruder says his background helped take it to the next level. “I’m an aerospace engineer. I started my career at NASA, working on power systems for planetary missions,” he said. There, he converted “heat energy into acoustic waves, then into power and cooling for a lander designed to survive on Venus.” That expertise was what lawyer Michael Thomas, the company’s co-founder and board chairman, was looking for to develop the technology, which he had been studying “as a side-project” since the 2000s. In 2019, after connecting on LinkedIn, the two founded Sonic Fire Tech, working “nights and weekends” around their full-time jobs on an early prototype. In 2025, they raised $3.5 million in funding, before a $15 million round in August 2026, led by the O.H.I.O. Fund. Testing and certification Dr. Michael J. Gollner, an associate professor of mechanical engineering at the University of California, Berkeley, who is chair of the Research Advisory Board of the NFPA Fire Protection Research Foundation, is familiar with the concept of using sound waves to extinguish fires. In 2015, he judged a thesis by a Berkeley student working on a similar technology. He sees promise, with limits. “At small scales and directed very close, the technology works well,” Gollner explained. “But whether it’s as efficient on big flames and in the long term still has to be proven.” He added that, despite the damage they can cause to a building once activated, “water suppression sprinklers are terribly efficient, and this new technology still needs to prove that it’s more efficient than this.” Today, Sonic Fire Tech employs around 20 people and is working toward certification. Interior fire suppression is already mandated in hundreds of local jurisdictions in the US, which gives the company a defined path to approval: in the short term, the Authority Having Jurisdiction — for example fire marshals — can approve individual installations. Sonic Fire Tech holds three permits in LA County and has begun its first installation in Altadena. This comes in the wake of the deadly Eaton Fire in 2025, which exposed infrastructure gaps where water shortages and dry hydrants hindered emergency response teams. The company has signed two reseller agreements with California home builders. In the longer term, a national lab must test and certify the system before it can be an option that architects and home builders can use for new homes — and potentially for businesses and data centers too. Bruder said certification testing was expected to begin this autumn, and they expect the first fire and safety certification in 2027. Fighting wildfires Last year, the San Bernardino County Fire Protection District participated in demonstrations with Sonic Fire Tech to evaluate the technology, including in-house simulation and wearable acoustic suppression backpacks. “Our personnel got to observe the technology and its capabilities, including possible applications for use by firefighters,” said Ryan Beckers, the San Bernardino County Fire Protection District public information officer. “We found the technology intriguing, particularly as a potential alternative to water-based home and industrial business sprinkler systems.” Beyond interior suppression, Sonic Fire Tech wants to eventually use sound waves to fight wildfires. In recent years, the US, and particularly California, has experienced devastating fires that have become easier to ignite and harder to contain as the result of a worsening climate crisis. The company hopes to alleviate the strain on water supplies without contributing to the environmental pollution associated with chemical retardants, which are often laden with toxic metals. Sonic Fire Tech has started a research project with the Cal Poly Wildland-Urban Interface (WUI) Fire Institute, the first step toward the full-scale testing insurers have asked for. “The fire situation in California really put people’s minds onto fire as a problem,” Bruder said. “The state really turned their attention to us once they realized how big a problem fire was and that water was not always going to be available.”

articles.title: 'Icarus' rise and fall': Analyst downgrades Nvidia stock amid Jensen Huang woes, highlights risks
articles.summary: Wall Street gets more cautious on Nvidia.
articles.body:
Let Wall Street analyst downgrades begin on the once-untouchable Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock in the wake of CEO Jensen Huang's high-profile affair.

Baird analyst Tristan Gerra cut his rating on Nvidia to Neutral on Wednesday in a note titled, "Icarus' Rise and Fall; Company Will be Fine."

"Downgrading to Neutral until uncertainties regarding U.S. government action likely resulting from the upcoming congressional hearing are lifted, U.S. government investigations reach their conclusions, revenue impact from risk channel near-term adjustments along with potential charges is quantified, and uncertainties around CEO tenure clear," Gerra wrote.

Huang admitted to the affair on Sunday in an email to employees. Shares are down about 12% since the situation became public.

Nvidia's board of directors launched an independent investigation into reports that the woman Huang had an affair with was allegedly a spy for the Chinese government.

The board said it hired powerful law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct the investigation. Former acting US Attorney of the Southern District of New York Joon Kim will run point on the investigation.

Gerra highlighted several near-term risks to Nvidia's stock, including a new ban on H200 exports to China.

"We believe low-level shipping is taking place into Asia-based warehouses with some inventories awaiting China demand. We estimate this could translate into a $5 billion write-down, Gerra said, adding: "Export control limitations notably addressing the Southeast Asia data center loopholes, along with DOJ potential action against Megaspeed and resulting preemptive or enforced actions from other data center operators located in the region with potential China demand exposure. Historically China-related GPU demand has been higher than Street expectations and often unquantified."

articles.title: Cement trader deposited Rs 14.74 lakh in his bank during demonetisation, but tax officer classified Rs 5.72 lakh as unexplained cash and sent notice; ITAT Cuttack deletes it after checking cash books
articles.summary: A cement trader based in Balasore, Odisha, came under the Income Tax Department's scrutiny after depositing Rs 14.74 lakh in cash into his bank account
articles.body: A cement trader based in Balasore, Odisha, came under the Income Tax Department's scrutiny after depositing Rs 14.74 lakh in cash into his bank account during the demonetisation period in November 2016.The Income Tax Assessing Officer (AO) in Balasore questioned the deposit and estimated the trader’s cement sales by comparing his business activity before and after demonetisation. Following this exercise, the AO classified Rs 5.72 lakh as unexplained cash and initiated proceedings against him.The trader, however, was unable to contest the department's action or file an appeal within the prescribed period because he had sustained a serious injury and was admitted to hospital. His doctor had advised him to remain on complete bed rest.After recovering, the trader approached the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Cuttack, to challenge the assessment, resulting in a delay of 736 days in filing the appeal.The tribunal condoned the delay and agreed to examine the case on its merits.Why did the cement trader win relief?The trader’s advocates submitted his cash books and other supporting evidence before ITAT Cuttack.They submitted that he had deposited Rs 14.74 lakh in cash into his bank account between November 30, 2016, and December 6, 2016. The Assessing Officer had classified Rs 5.72 lakh of this amount as “unexplained cash”. However, the cash book maintained for the cement business showed that he had Rs 14.78 lakh available in cash as of November 8, 2016, they argued.According to the advocates, the cash book established that the trader had sufficient recorded cash on the date of demonetisation to account for the subsequent bank deposits. They therefore contended that the penalty order should be set aside.According to an ET report, after examining the facts, ITAT Cuttack found that the man had an adequate cash balance on the date of demonetisation to make the deposits into his bank account.The tribunal also noted that the AO had neither rejected the books of account maintained for the cement business nor disputed the net profit reported in the profit and loss account.Explaining its decision, ITAT Cuttack said: “Once the books of accounts have been accepted, the cash available as of the date of demonitisation and SBN (specified bank note) deposits are less than the cash availability as of the date of demonitisation, we are of the view that no addition is called for in the hands of the assessee. Consequently, the addition made by the AO and confirmed by ld CIT(A) stands deleted.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: After Mother Dairy, Amul hikes milk prices by up to Rs 4 per litre from November 12
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Milk prices are set to rise from Thursday, November 12, with dairy majors Amul and Mother Dairy increasing rates by Rs 2 to Rs 4 per litre
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Milk prices are set to rise from Thursday, November 12, with dairy majors Amul and Mother Dairy increasing rates by Rs 2 to Rs 4 per litre across several variants.Gujarat Co-operative Milk Marketing Federation (GCMMF), which markets dairy products under the Amul brand, announced a 4-5% increase in the prices of fresh pouch milk across major variants and pack sizes in India. Mother Dairy has also revised the prices of its liquid milk variants by Rs 2-4 per litre, according to PTI reports.Both companies have cited higher input and procurement costs for the increase. The revisions come around six months after their previous price hikes in May.In a statement on Wednesday, GCMMF said the revised prices would take effect on November 12, 2026. "The price of our largest-selling Amul Taaza toned milk with 3 per cent milk fat has been increased by only Rs 2 per litre (3.3 per cent increase) and Amul Gold Milk with 6 per cent milk fat by Rs 4 per litre (5.5 per cent rise)," the federation said.It said the hike followed a sharp rise in the cost of milk production and processing. Expenses on green and dry fodder, cattle feed ingredients such as oil cake, maize and molasses, packaging film and fuel have increased significantly over the past year."In the current challenging environmental circumstances due to low and uneven rainfall in Gujarat, as well as many parts of India, we are constrained to increase the consumer price of milk to pay better prices to our producers and support them in these difficult times," it added.GCMMF said its member unions had raised procurement prices paid to farmers by 4-5% over the past year. It added that a further revision would help support milk producers.The federation said around 80% of the revenue earned from consumers through the Amul co-operative structure is returned to 36 lakh milk producers. It added that a major share of the latest retail price increase would also go to farmers.Mother Dairy has also increased the prices of its liquid milk variants by Rs 2-4 per litre from November 12, according to PTI.The company, the largest milk supplier in Delhi-NCR, last revised prices on May 14, 2026. Sources said higher procurement costs had prompted the latest increase, with the company passing on part of the additional burden to consumers.In Delhi-NCR, the price of toned milk sold in bulk vending machines has been raised to Rs 60 per litre from Rs 58. Full-cream pouch milk will now cost Rs 76 per litre, up from Rs 72, while pouch toned milk will cost Rs 62, compared with Rs 60 earlier.The price of double-toned milk has increased to Rs 56 per litre from Rs 54, while cow milk will cost Rs 65 per litre, up from Rs 62.Mother Dairy sells around 35 lakh litres of milk daily in the Delhi-NCR market through its outlets, general trade and e-commerce platforms. Its total daily milk sales exceed 50 lakh litres. The company said it passes on 75-80% of its milk sales realisation to farmers.The latest revision will increase household spending on an essential food item and could add to inflationary pressures. The impact will depend on the extent to which consumers adjust their purchases and spending.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Nvidia stock rebounds, chip stocks surge as CoreWeave earnings boost AI trade
articles.summary: Nvidia stock popped on Wednesday, snapping a two-day losing streak.
articles.body:
Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock rebounded on Wednesday as the overall chip sector surged on the heels of CoreWeave's ( CRWV ) better-than-expected quarterly results.

Nvidia shares rose for the first time since CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, rising roughly 2% after two straight days of declines. A company board investigation , increased scrutiny from lawmakers , and questions over whether restricted semiconductors were diverted to China have weighed on the stock in recent sessions.

Even with the bounce, Nvidia is down about 14% in November and has lost about $700 billion in market value. The rally also came despite a downgrade on the stock from Baird to Neutral.

"Downgrading to Neutral until uncertainties regarding U.S. government action likely resulting from the upcoming congressional hearing are lifted, U.S. government investigations reach their conclusions, revenue impact from risk channel near-term adjustments along with potential charges is quantified, and uncertainties around CEO tenure clear," analyst Tristan Gerra wrote in a note to clients.

The broader semiconductor sector jumped on Wednesday after CoreWeave raised its full-year revenue outlook to $13 billion to $13.3 billion, up from a prior target of $12 billion to $13 billion, citing strong demand for AI compute capacity.

"Demand for compute is growing faster than the capacity to deliver that infrastructure and that is being echoed by the expansion of the margins that we are seeing on each additional contract," CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said during the company's earnings call on Tuesday.

Shares of chipmakers AMD ( AMD ) and Broadcom ( AVGO ) stock rose over 5%, while Intel ( INTC ) shares surged.

Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company ( TSM ), which manufactures Nvidia chips, jumped 4%. Semiconductor equipment maker ASML ( ASML ) rose 3%.
