When people discuss investment strategies, Warren Buffett's name is likely to come up.

One of America's most successful investors, Buffett generated an average annual return of nearly 19% for Berkshire Hathaway shareholders over more than 60 years. That's well above the S&P 500 index's ( ^GSPC ) nearly 11% gain over the same period.

His philosophy: Buy undervalued stocks for companies with strong financial fundamentals.

However, for the average investor, he recommends just the opposite. For those who don't have the time or inclination to research companies and maintain a portfolio, he suggests low-cost index funds and what many experts might consider an aggressive allocation: 90% in equities and 10% in short-term government bonds.

Can the typical, novice investor stick to the high commitment to equities that the 90/10 portfolio advises when the market is down sharply?

Ryan Dykmans, CFA, president and chief investment officer at Dunham & Associates Investment Counsel in San Diego, believes the 90/10 portfolio may be best for a certain kind of investor.

"I have a great deal of respect for Buffett, but the 'average' investor may not have Buffett's time horizon, liquidity, or temperament and discipline," Dykmans told Yahoo Finance. "For a younger investor with decades ahead and the ability to remain invested, a 90/10 allocation could maximize long-term gains. But for someone nearing retirement, drawing income from the portfolio, or likely to lose sleep and force an emotional strategy change during a major decline — it may be too aggressive."

Higher equity exposure may improve long-term return potential, he added, but also comes with sharper drawdowns. "Ultimately, the right allocation has to fit the individual investor, including not only their ability to take risk, but also their willingness to take risk."

He said there is also a "human side" to consider.

"Research shows people feel losses much more harshly than equivalent gains — the old adage of 'the pain of a loss outweighs the joy of a gain.' That reaction can become even more powerful during a major market decline when an investor is 90% invested in stocks."

Dykmans believes the best allocation is one an investor can live with and stick to even when the market news is at its worst.

Buffett's take on down stock markets is often quoted: "You want to be greedy when others are fearful. You want to be fearful when others are greedy."

Dykmans believes that advice is still useful.

"It addresses the hardest part of investing — managing emotions. We believe discipline matters most when markets are testing it," he added. "I would also add two more Buffett principles: 'Look for a margin of safety, and do not confuse a rising price with lower risk.' Markets can become overly optimistic or overly pessimistic. A sound process helps investors avoid chasing either extreme."

Buffett also stressed that the most important quality for an investor "is temperament, not intellect."

"Following those rules, the 'know-nothing' investor who both diversifies and keeps his costs minimal is virtually certain to get satisfactory results," Buffett wrote in his 2013 letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders. "Indeed, the unsophisticated investor who is realistic about his shortcomings is likely to obtain better long-term results than the knowledgeable professional who is blind to even a single weakness."

articles.title: Can Tehran survive a ‘zero oil’ budget, if US blockade on Iran persists?
articles.summary: The government is defiant and planning for the worst, but a US siege is expected to make most Iranians poorer.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – After months of oscillating between new bouts of fighting and negotiations, the administration of United States President Donald Trump has reportedly opted for a third option – gradual economic pressure on Tehran.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told his Group of Seven (G7) counterparts in Paris on Tuesday that a naval blockade, stringent sanctions and overland border disruptions could continue without a clear endpoint in sight, according to US media. He later said that Iran’s economy “continues to collapse” and predicted worsening conditions over the next one to three months.

Tehran-based economist and market analyst Isaac Saidian said that if the persistent economic siege on Iran brings the country’s oil incomes down to near-zero levels, Tehran will be faced with one of the most difficult challenges in its recent history.

“The issue is not just a decline in foreign currency incomes, but the government’s ability to account for current expenditure, paying salaries and pensions, providing essential goods, preserving the value of the national currency, and preventing budget deficits from turning into a new inflationary wave,” Saidian told Al Jazeera.

Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian has indicated that the cash-strapped civilian government is preparing to deal with a prolonged economic crisis caused by siege and sanctions, but has admitted that the lingering “no war, no peace” conditions will be harmful.

But the authorities have stressed that there are no prospects of economic collapse . They have also raised the prospect of “breaking the blockade” if necessary, although it remains unclear by what means.

In a budget directive on November 3, Pezeshkian’s administration set out two scenarios. One was the continuation of sanctions, the maritime blockade and present regional conditions. The other prediction was an improvement of the situation involving fewer financial and commercial restrictions, including a substantial or complete removal of the blockade.

“The government must prepare for circumstances in which oil revenue reaches zero,” Mohammad Ghasemi, deputy for coordination of planning and budget at Iran’s Plan and Budget Organization, told local media on Monday about a contingency for next year.

The US military first imposed a naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports, through which most of the country’s trade passed, on April 13. A memorandum of understanding in June lifted the blockade and allowed some oil and trade to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, but the deal fell apart within weeks. The second blockade has been in place since July 14, as Iran and the US fight for control of the Strait of Hormuz.

The US military says it has redirected 147 ships and disabled five while enforcing the blockade. It also claimed to have destroyed 10 Iranian oil tankers linked to the shadow fleet of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). According to the US Treasury, the blockade has led to Iran loading no oil onto vessels since August 25.

A late October assessment by Kpler said Iran’s oil production had fallen below 2 million barrels a day in the preceding months. Iran produced 3.45 million barrels of crude per day in January and 3.59 million in the following month, but Israel and the US’s war on Iran began on February 28.

The volume of Iranian crude and condensate floating outside the blockade zone had also fallen from 88.8 million barrels on July 14 to zero in mid-October. Because Chinese buyers generally pay one to two months after discharge, Kpler anticipated crude and condensate receipts potentially drying up around mid-December. Around 43 million barrels remain stranded inside the blockade area.

The US sanctions have also limited air travel to and from Iran, while a new US task force announced this week aims at closing or disrupting most of Iran’s land borders with its seven neighbours.

The Iranian economy has already been dealing with chronic inflation, falling investments and purchasing power, as well as banking and budget imbalances for years. So removing oil revenues will undoubtedly exacerbate the situation.

The government has increasingly relied on taxes to account for a larger share of the budget, but oil still accounted for roughly one-third of planned government funding in the 2026–27 budget proposal.

Economist Saidian said if oil revenues fall sharply, the government’s next step should be to review public spending. Cutting spending on overlapping administrative structures and opaque budgetary grants, while suspending low-return public investment projects, could ease some of the fiscal pressure on the state, he said.

Reforming tax exemptions and tackling tax evasion, as well as carefully managed bond issuance and sale of some non-essential government assets, are other options. But he cautioned that any abrupt drops in salaries, pensions, or social support budgets would only deepen poverty.

The government has signalled that it will likely have to resort to reducing fuel and other energy subsidies again, which will increase prices, but the process will be gradual to lessen the impact on inflation.

“Expanding non-oil exports and facilitating trade with neighbouring countries are also essential,” Saidian said. “Even so, these exports cannot be expected to replace oil revenue in the short term, especially while restrictions on banking, insurance and transport remain in place.”

Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani said on Tuesday that next year’s budget would prioritise inflation control through fiscal discipline, household support and tighter oversight of banks. The administration will continue handing out electronic food coupons, although it has been struggling to preserve their value due to runaway prices.

Year-on-year inflation was at nearly 89 percent in the Iranian calendar month ending October 22, according to the Statistical Center of Iran.

Saidian pointed out that no amount of austerity measures or budget reforms can fully replace sustainable access to foreign trade, investment and foreign currency incomes, so exiting inflationary stagnation for a prolonged period would require reduced tensions.

“The historical significance of the 2027-28 budget lies in what it can reveal about how prepared Iran’s government is to move beyond an oil-dependent economy and toward transparent, accountable fiscal governance. The budget should not merely be a plan to manage the government in a difficult year, but a plan to prevent passing on today’s crisis to future generations and to start structural reforms in Iran’s economy,” he said.

“The greatest danger is not that the government might run short of funds for a few months. The real danger is that it could stay afloat on paper while passing the cost of doing so on to the public, leaving society poorer, eroding the middle class, widening poverty and weakening the country’s productive capacity.”

articles.title: Wall Street is cooling on Jensen Huang's Nvidia — but history says don't give up on the stock just yet
articles.summary: Morgan Stanley and Bank of America pulled Nvidia from their best-ideas lists, but nearly all analysts still rate the stock a Buy.
articles.body:
Breaking up with Nvidia ( NVDA ) is hard to do. After the stock dropped 25%, two of Wall Street's biggest banks pulled it from their top-pick lists, and neither could bring itself to say "sell" — yet.

Morgan Stanley's version was the most polite: It's not you, it's our stop-loss policy. The bank removes any top pick that falls more than 25% from where it was named, and Nvidia had slid a bit more since getting the title on Oct. 2. Only a day earlier, Bank of America cut Nvidia, Micron ( MU ) and Lam Research ( LRCX ) from its US 1 List of best ideas. Both banks still rate Nvidia a Buy.

Others were less gentle. Baird cut the stock to Neutral on Wednesday and slashed its price target to $200 from $500, citing rising odds of a CEO change. Aletheia Capital downgraded Nvidia to Hold on Monday. Mizuho, Citi, and Wells Fargo trimmed their price targets in the days after reports tied CEO Jensen Huang to a suspected Chinese spy .

Still, nobody is packing Nvidia's things into a box. Of 82 analysts who rate the stock, 77 call it a Buy, according to Bloomberg data.

The average price target sits about 87% above where the stock closed Tuesday. That's the widest gap between the two measures in two years of monthly readings, because the stock fell and the targets mostly stayed put.

Wall Street's reluctance to get bearish on Nvidia has history on its side, mostly.

Nvidia has closed 25% below a record 13 times since its 1999 IPO. A year later, it was higher in nine of them, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.

The exceptions were brutal. After drops in 2001, 2002, and 2007, the stock lost more than half its value again over the next 12 months. It's also a small sample, and half of it comes from the dot-com boom and bust, when Nvidia was a fraction of today's $4 trillion giant.

Even Bank of America's own strategist isn't giving up on the bigger AI story. "It's paramount for the US to remain number one in terms of tech primacy. And that's where I see almost a put on the ... tech story," Savita Subramanian, BofA's head of US equity and quantitative strategy, told Yahoo Finance on Tuesday — though she didn't discuss the list change itself.

Analysts have been right lately. Every average target set from November 2024 through November 2025 was reached within a year, according to Yahoo Finance analysis of Bloomberg data.

And Nvidia is no longer priced for perfection. It trades at about 11 times next fiscal year's expected earnings, per Yahoo Finance calculations, versus about 18 times for the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ), according to FactSet.

articles.title: Anthropic's IPO has a line around the block. History says that's not the signal to watch.
articles.summary: From Meta to SpaceX, big order books haven't spared new stocks a rough first year.
articles.body:
There's a line outside Anthropic's IPO, and the bankers want everyone to see it. Any nightclub owner knows the crowd outside says more about the door than the party.

Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) offering has drawn multiple times the orders for the shares available, Bloomberg reported Wednesday, led by anchor-size orders. With a private placement , Anthropic and its co-founders are raising as much as about $90 billion at a targeted $1.4 trillion valuation , which would make it the biggest listing ever.

Saudi Aramco ( 2222.SR ) drew nearly five times the shares on offer in 2019, or $119 billion of bids for a $26 billion sale. SpaceX ( SPCX ) pulled in more than $250 billion of demand for its June debut, about four times the deal. Facebook, now Meta ( META ), and Rivian ( RIVN ) had packed books too. Both were down roughly 40% to 70% a year after their first-day open, by Yahoo Finance calculations.

Most IPOs are heavily oversubscribed, which lets underwriters pick who gets shares , according to University of Florida professor Jay Ritter. Investors know it, so they pad their orders on hot deals, expecting them to be cut back in size. Plenty of that demand is often fast money looking for a quick flip.

That's why the first month of trading can mislead. "For the first 30 days you've got a pop with the IPO, but then after the lockup , that's when the market's actually going to give us the true valuation," Robert Schein, chief investment officer at Blanke Schein Wealth Management, told Yahoo Finance.

Still, the order book isn't worthless. It just speaks through the price.

Since 1980, US IPOs priced above their marketed range have gained 50% on day one on average, according to Ritter's data . Deals priced within the range averaged 12%, and those priced below it just 3%. Only about a quarter of deals clear that bar.

Anthropic set its $70-$78 range conservatively, and the Financial Times reported that bankers now expect to price above it, lifting the valuation to $1.5 trillion or more. Pricing is expected Nov. 18, with trading as soon as Nov. 19. When the bouncers start raising the cover charge, the crowd outside is real.

IPOs from 1980 to 2024 returned about 6% on average in their first year, compared with about 11% for similar-size companies. They trailed in four of their first five years. That's one reason four centuries of hot IPOs have rewarded patience more than speed.

articles.title: Nvidia stock rebounds as scrutiny into Huang mounts
articles.summary: Nvidia’s stock rebounded on Wednesday morning, as the company probes and lawmakers scrutinize CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Shares of the company were up roughly 3.4 percent as of the late morning, trading at above $174 per share. Nvidia’s stock closed below $169 per share on Tuesday, reaching a six-month low…
articles.body:
Nvidia’s stock rebounded on Wednesday morning, as the company probes and lawmakers scrutinize CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Shares of the company were up roughly 3.4 percent as of the late morning, trading at above $174 per share. Nvidia’s stock closed below $169 per share on Tuesday, reaching a six-month low of $165.89 during intraday trading.

Nvidia’s board of directors opened an investigation into Huang on Sunday, after The New York Times reported on Oct. 29 he had a “close relationship” with Alice Huang — no relation — whom U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy.

The board announced Tuesday that it had hired Joon H. Kim, the former acting U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, to lead the probe. Kim, the board said, will conduct a “thorough and independent investigation” into the matter.

Jensen Huang admitted to an affair in a company memo, Bloomberg reported Sunday, although he did not mention Alice Huang.

Lawmakers on Capitol Hill are citing Huang’s affair with the alleged spy as justification for restricting exports of Nvidia’s chips, which power artificial intelligence hardware.

“It is time for Congress to take decisive action to pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the NDAA that will cut off pathways through which China accesses advanced chips,” Sens. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said Monday in a joint statement.

Nvidia will also report third-quarter earnings next Tuesday. The company previously reported $96.2 billion in revenue for the second quarter of this year, up 106 percent from the second quarter of 2025.

articles.title: CoreWeave stock pops — but its debt problem hasn't gone anywhere
articles.summary: Investors may want to temper their CoreWeave enthusiasm.
articles.body:
Investors may want to temper their CoreWeave ( CRWV ) enthusiasm, which is on full display Wednesday.

This is far from a perfect business, and don't lose sight of that.

CoreWeave stock popped 24% in morning trading as the company came out swinging against the bears that have shredded the stock more than 40% inside of a month.

The company beat on third quarter sales estimates . Its loss was better than expected. It raised the bottom end of full-year revenue guidance by $1 billion.

Less than 30 minutes into the earnings call, CEO Michael Intrator even attempted to take the bears head-on again.

"Looking ahead, we will not use the unsecured debt market to fund our business at current yields, nor do we need to," Intrator said. "Consistent with our historical approach, we expect to finance the majority of the remaining CapEx needed to deliver our backlog through delayed draw term loans matched to specific customer contracts. Through 2027, more than 75% of committed CapEx is tied to investment-grade and enterprise customers, with the remainder tied to the world's leading AI labs and AI-native companies. The pricing of these facilities reflects the underlying customer commitments and our proven ability to deliver. They can finance anywhere from 70%-100% of the associated CapEx,"

But all of this doesn't sweep this important issue under the rug regarding CoreWeave: It has a lot of debt and an insane amount of associated interest expense!

For the nine months ended Sept. 30, CoreWeave's interest expense tallied $2 billion — up sharply from $841 million a year earlier. The excessive interest expense easily toppled the $14 million in operating income CoreWeave generated in the same period.

In the third quarter alone, CoreWeave racked up $846 million in interest expense.

The company's non-current recourse debt ballooned to $32.4 billion from $14.6 billion a year earlier.

In short, CoreWeave needs a lot to go right over the next 12 months to support a balance sheet that's throwing off this high level of interest expense.

"CoreWeave delivered about the best quarter we could have asked for," Bernstein analyst Madison Rezaei said. "They're continuing to mature as a company, executing better with every print, and managing the narrative more competently than they ever have. Stats were good-to-great, funding concerns were addressed, the strategic moves make sense, and, much as we were after 2Q earnings, we're left grappling with our Underperform. We want to be believers, especially with the stock off 65% from its May high. If we were sitting in Intrator's chair, we'd make many of the same calls, and we congratulate the CRWV team on the trajectory. But we just can't get over our long-term fundamental concerns about this business model."

CoreWeave's business was — and is — reliant on customers, and markets have confidence in the model working as designed. Expect said confidence to continue to be tested.

articles.title: US credit card debt reaches a record $1.3 trillion as inflation rises
articles.summary: Americans are struggling to keep up with higher prices, and they're putting larger balances on their credit cards.
articles.body:
Americans are leaning on credit cards to keep up with higher prices, with October's headline inflation data coming in hotter than expected.

In a new report from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, US credit card balances rose by $22 billion in the third quarter, reaching a record $1.28 trillion dollars in total debt. This increase came as inflation measured by the Consumer Price Index rose by 0.4% in October from the previous month.

Prices for key essentials like groceries increased 0.4% month over month after remaining relatively flat over the past two months. Americans also paid more for gas, fuel, and electricity, up 1%, 2.4%, and 0.9%, respectively, compared to the month before and on top of modest gains in previous months.

The national average credit card interest rate currently stands at 19.71%, per Bankrate , the highest interest rate level since December 2025. That's likely causing Americans to accrue debt faster. Plus, Americans tend to take on more debt around the holidays, with US consumers planning to spend over $1 trillion during the key holiday months this year, according to the National Retail Federation.

Americans "continue to spend, despite high gas prices and the lowest sentiment we've ever seen, so it doesn't surprise us that that's going to carry through the holiday season," Ali Furman, PwC US consumer markets industry leader, told Yahoo Finance in September. "It's just a continuation of the trends."

Delinquency rates, or the rate of people with overdue payments, worsened in the third quarter too, increasing by 0.3 percentage points from the previous quarter to 6.87%.

It's not just credit card debt that Americans are finding themselves in; higher rates on mortgage, auto, and student loans are also taking a toll.

Mortgage balances increased by $257 billion last quarter, totaling $13.4 trillion at the end of September. The average price of a home in the US is now near $500,000 after spiking around this time last year, according to St. Louis Fed data .

Auto loan balances jumped by $21 billion in Q3 to $1.73 trillion as new vehicle prices hit a record high of $51,000 in October, according to Kelley Blue Book.

Student loan balances also grew by $5 billion, bringing the total to $1.66 trillion in debt for Americans as tuition continues to climb each month.

Higher interest rates may be here to stay, making it harder for Americans to pay off the debt. Based on the hotter-than-expected October inflation reading, the Fed is expected to raise interest rates at its policy meeting next month.
